THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI YASHWANT SINHA): Sir, I do

transparency or it is an interference or conspiracy on the part of certain officials.

Board for this purpose, which is headed by the Governor, RBI. A Comm ittee

transparent norms, had invited 63 Chief General Managers from various public

will be allowed to come in the way of this procedure. It is absolutely a merit -
based consideration.

Recovery suit against Essar Power Ltd. 
*504. SHRI R. S. GAVAI: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the recovery suit file by Andhra Bank against 
Essar Power Ltd; is pending with the Debt Recovery Tribunal at Mumbai; 
(b) if so, the details thereof, alongwith the amount sanctioned as loan to 
the company, 
(c) the steps taken by Andhra Bank for recovery of loan before filing the 
suit; and 
(d) the reaction of Essar Power Ltd., thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY O F FINANCE 
(SHRI BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the 
Table of the House. 
STATEMENT 
(a) and (b) Yes, Sir. Andhra Bank has filed a recovery application before 
the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT), Mumbai on 31st August, 1999 for the 
recovery of outstanding dues of Essar Power Limited. The application is pending 
before DRT, Mumbai. The application has been filed for recovery of balance 
outstanding dues amounting to Rs 17.70 crore against the loan of Rs 50 crore 
sanctioned to the company in 1994. 
11 

RAJYA SABHA [02 MAY, 2000]

further reported that the company has made another part payment of Rs 6.00 
crore after filing of the recovery application before DRT.

Propagation of Satriya Dance and Music 
*505. DR. ARUN KUMAR SARMA : Will the Minister of CULTURE 
be pleased to state : 
(a) the origin and status of Satriya Dance as a component of Indian 
Classical Art forms; 
(b) the steps initiated by Government to promote Satriya Dance and 
Music of Assam and future plans, if any, on research and training; 
(c) the details of the programme finalised incl uding publication of 
photo illustrations etc. by the Centre for Cultural Resources and Training for 
propagation of Satriya Dance and Music; and 
(d) the action initiated for adequate exposure of this dance form through 
various performances in India and abroad? 
THE MINISTER OF CULTURE (SHRI ANANTH KUMAR) : (a) 
According to scholars the Satriya Dance originated towards the end of the 15th 
or early 16th century. The dance and music forms of Satriya constitute an 
important segment of the performing arts heritage of our country. 
(b) The Sangeet Natak Akademi has taken steps to promote and preserve 
Satriya Dance through financial grants, audio/video documentation of Satriya 
Dance and allied forms, sponsoring performances, promoting interaction 
between Satriya artistes and masters of other dance traditions and grant of awards 
and fellowships. 
(c) The Centre for Cultural Resources and Training has produced a 
documentary film on Satriya Dance and has also prepared colour slides and 
photographs. 
(d) From time to time the Sangeet Natak Akademi has sponsored 
performances of Satriya Dance in their festivals and events held within India.  
The Indian Council for Cultural Relations had sponsored a performance of  
Satriya Dance in USA in 1998.

Minister is indicative of the fact that due justice was not extended to this very 
old traditional classical dance of Assam, i.e. the Satriya Dance. The origin of

[02 MAY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA

(a) to (c) Recognising the magnitude and complexity of the problem, the 
Government of India constituted the Brahmaputra  Board in December, 1981 
under the Brahmaputra Board Act, 1980 for planning and implementation of 
measures for the management of floods and bank erosion in Brahmaputra valley. 
The major activities of the Board arc preparation of Master Plans and 
investigation of projects in the Brahmaputra and Barak basins.

Management in Brahmaputra and Barak valleys and their tributaries. 22 no.

Tipaimukh Dam Project has been entrusted to North -Eastern Electric Power

States for implementation by the State Governments from the  funds allocated

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMUNI -
CATIONS (SHRI TAPANI SIKDAR) (a) Postal services in the entire country 
including rural areas arc provided by the Department of Posts as per provisions 
of Indian Post Office Act. 1898 and Rules framed thereunder According to 
these statutory provisions, the Department of Posts has monopoly in the matter 
of letter mail articles only. 
(b) and (c) Extra Departmental Agents (EDAs) numbering 3,09. 915 as 
on 31- 3-99 arc responsible for the entire rural postal not work Comprising 
1.28.193 ED Post Offices in the country, The Extra-Departmental System which 
is more than a century old has proved its worth as a practical and viable method 
of extending basic postal facilities to rural areas where due to inadequate work-
load full-fledged departmental posts offices cannot be set up. The ED Agents 
arc engaged on specific terms and conditions which vary significantly from' 
those of regular Govt employees. ED Agents arc required to work for a period 
of 2 to 5 hours per day only and it is necessary for them to have alternate source 
of independent livelihood. Being local residents of the post village or the 
delivery jurisdiction of the Branch Post Office, they enjoy accep tability in the 
local community they serve. ED Post Office provides all basic postal services 
including agency functions which arc of benefit to the rural population and 
help in socio-economic development 
Terms and conditions of engagement for ED Agents ha ve been revised 
from time to time by the Government progressively extending allowances and 
other payments on pro-rata and resulting in additional benefits for ED Agents 
In the context of setting up of the Vth Central pay Commission Tor regular 
Central Gove rnment employees, the Government had set up a one man 
committee headed by Justice Charanjit Talwar, retired judge. Delhi High Court 
to examine the wage structure and service condition of ED Agents and the 
Committee submitted its report to the Government on  30-4-97. After due 
consideration of the recommendations of justice Talwar Committee, the 
Government extended a package of benefits to ED Agents in full and final 
settlement of all pending demands relating to implementation of just ice Talwar 
Committee's recommendations. This package of benefits extended through the 
order of Department of Posts dated 17-12-98 provided the following additional 
benefits lor the ED Agents:—  
(i) Payment of arrears for the period 1 -1-1996 to 28- 2-1998 by 
increasing the basic allowance of ED Agents by multiplying it with 
a factor of 3.25

pattern of first two scales of pay recommended by the Justice Talwar 
Committee for each category of ED Agents (except ED SPMs for 
which only one TRCA). 
(iii) Provision of paid leave for 10 days for each half year, without the 
facility of earn- forward. 
(iv) Increased limit of ex -gratia gratuity for ED Agents from Rs. 6000/ - 
to Rs 18.000/-. 
(v) Increased amount of Office maintenance Allowance from Rs. 25/-per 
month to Rs. 50/- per month for EDBPMs. and EDSPMs. 
(vi) Payment of lumpsum Severance Amount of Rs. 20.000/ - or Rs. 
30.000/- depending on period of employ ment of ED Agents, on 
demitting office at the age of 65 years or after absorption against 
regular departmental post, as a form of post employment benefits. 
Recommendations made by justice Talwar Committee also including those for 
rationalising the ED system, reducing the number of ED Agents and also capping 
future growth of the system. But appreciating the relevance of the ED System for 
the rural postal network and its social benefits. Government have not implemented 
these recommendations. The Government's policy therefore, ensures full justice to 
the interest of ED Agents. The benefits extended to the ED As through order dated

3872 SHRI H. K. JAVARE GOWDA : Will the Minister of FINANCE

application forms, delegation of powers to the branch managers of banks for 
speedier sanction of loan, insistence of no -due certificate by banks at their 
own discretion, non- insistence of security/ margin for agricultural loans upto 
Rs. 10,000/- etc. In addition, banks falling short of their target in lending to 
agriculture have to contribut e to Rural Infrastructure Development Fund

Corporation for completion of their on- going projects relating to rural

STATEMENT 
I. Cental Water Comnussion 
 
The Central Water Commission is charged with the general responsibility  of 
initiating, coordinating and furthering in consultation with the  
StateGovernments concerned, schemes for the control, conservation and 
utilisation of water resources throughout the country for the purpose of flood 
manager irrigation, navigation, drinking water supply and water power 
generation. The Commission will, if so requires also undertake the  construction 
and execution   of any such scheme In exercise of these responsibilities the 
Central Water Commission is performing the following function:- 
                 1. To make all necessary investigations and surveys and when so  
                      required, to prepare schemes and designs for the development of

rehabilitation and resettlement, soil conservation, anti-water logging

related facilities such as malaria control, recreation and fish culture 
and —  for drinking water supply; 
2. to undertaken construction work of any river valley development scheme 
on behalf of the Government of India or State Governments concerned;

investigation, surveys and preparation of river valley and power

precious rain water as Scientists have forecasted that India in the  next

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY O F WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY) : (a) to (c) Rainfall 
in the country is highly variable both in time and space. This results in floods in 
some parts of the country, whereas the other parts arc affected by droughts. 
About 40  +7Mha of the area in the country is flood prone whereas 51.13 Mha 
is drought prone. On an average 7.5 Mha area is affected annually by floods 
with average damages of the order of Rs. 1,155 crore. On an average 1, 529 
human lives are lost due to floods. India receives an average annual rainfall of 
about 4000 Billion Cubic Meter (BCM) including snow. Out of this, 3, 000 
BCM occurs during monsoon resulting in an average annual flow of about 1869 
BCM in the various rivers of the country. The utilisable runoff by 
conventional methods has been assessed as 690 Billion Cubic Meter (BCM). 
A live storage capacity of 176.73 BCM has been created by construction of 
large dams upto 1995 including about 3 BCM capacity created by medium & 
small dams. Projects to add an additional capacity of about 75.42 BCM are under 
construction and 132.32 BCN are under planning. Out of 432 BCM of 
replenishable ground water, 260 BCM has been tapped. In order to complete 
the ongoing projects, Government is providing Central Loan Assistance 
underAccelerated Irrigation Benefit Programme. The National Water Policy 
(1987) stipulates that drinking water requirement should be the first charge on 
any available water. In addition, Command Area Development Programme is 
being implemented to fully utilize the potential created. 
Government of India is also promoting Rain Water Harvesting through 
Watershed Management Programme, Artificial Recharge of Ground Water and 
roof-top rain water harvesting under the Sector reform Project of Accelerated 
Rural Water Supply Programme under the Ministry of Rural Development for 
which technical and financial assistance is provided to the State Government 
and other implementing agencies. Central Ground Water Board has also taken 
up pilot studies for artificial ground water recharge.

STATEMENT 
The main recommendations of the National Commission for Integrated 
Water Resources Development are as under :—  
1. Continued Government funding on enhanced scale for major 
projects, instilling financial discipline and prioritisation of projects 
for channelising the funds. Central assistance to major projects to 
be project-wise instead of being part of the overall plan assistance. 
2. Need for well laid down compensation packages for all categories of 
project affected persons. While doing so, the Commission has 
emphasised that resettlement and rehabilitation projects be 
implemented by a functional authority with sufficient funds. 
3. Need for amending the existing Inter -State Water Disputes Act, 
1956, enactment of a new Act in lieu of the existing River Board's 
Act, 1956, and also amending the existing Irrigation Acts which 
would facilitate participatory irrigation management. 
4. Optimal utilisation of land and water should be aimed at in basins 
having surplus before considering interbasin transfers (intrabasin 
transfer to be given first priority). 
5. Setting up of River Basin Organisation for  each Inter -State River 
having representation from the concerned State Governments, 
Water Users etc. 
6. Substantial revision of present water rates to cover the entire 
operation & maintainance expenses, constituting Water Pricing 
Authority on the analogy of existing Energy Pricing Authorities. 
160 

[02 MAY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
7. For Environment protection, the principle of "User Pays, Polluter Pays" 
need to be adopted for industrial uses. 
8. Need for reviewing the National Water Policy (1987), need for making 
hydrological data for all basins freely available to all interested. 
9. For flood control measures, Commission has recommended 
preparation of disaster preparedness plans, performance review of 
embankments and policy to regulate the land use in different flood zones. 
Existing flood forcecasting system be strengthened and modernised 
using telemetry and satellite communication. 
 
10. For optimal and integrated development of trans— Himalayan rivers, India 
should work for cooperation amongst the neighbouring countries. For 
this purpose, it has been suggested that National Water Development Agency 
(NWDA) in India, Water Resource Planning Organisations (WARPO) in 
Bangladesh and Energy Development Authority (EDA) in Nepal be 
designated to interact as a clearing house of information. 
11. For hydropower development, Commission has recommended creation 
of hydropower development fund, promotion of joint ventures, tariff 
rationalisation etc. 
12. For navigation development, the Commission has recommended that Inland 
Water Transport be treated as a nascent industry.

DR. RAJA RAMANNA (Nominated): Sir, it is with great sadness that 
I take part in this debate on Air India. In the earlier days, we used to be so 
proud of our national carrier and it was thought to be a part of our 
Independence Movement. In those days, our airline system was among the 
best in the world. We used to be so proud of it. At that time, the Chairman was 
no less a person than Mr. J.R.D. Tata. Now, as the years go by, it is easy to 
forget Mr. Tata. But we have seen him in action, in running the various 
industries of the country and in looking after Air India. He was not a full time 
Chairman. We were very proud of the fact that Air India was by far the best 
airline in the world. We did ask  him once: How do you manage to keep Air 
India at such a high position? And we were very surprised with the reply that 
he gave. He said, "I give top priority to maintenance." People think that it is 
the management, or. sending off the files quickly. or. the amount of money 
involved, that is important. But you must appoint the right people to see that 
the plane is maintained regularly and the signals are checked regularly. When 
a plane comes down, it should come down with a natural safety. The people 
had a kind of pride in running these planes. This was obvious to all of us who 
travelled in those days. Everybody was polite on the plane. Even the 
passengers wanted to look after the plane and not mess it up. as they do it 
now. All this comes about due to a widespread lack of morale. If something 
goes wrong, everything starts going wrong and even the passengers become 
a nuisance, as it happened in recent times. But I would like to bring to the 
attention of the people that simply saying that the management is bad,  will not 
do. Management can be wonderful, but the management has to be built up. I 
can give you hundreds of instances where planes have flown empty and 
ticketing people have been rude to me and say that we cannot take you even 
when I have a reservation . But the basic malaise must be understood. For 
instance. Mr. Tata was ignominiously removed from the Chairmanship by no 
less than a great Prime Minister like Mr. Morarji Desai. There was a strange 
reason for  it.     He said.  "We should have a chairman  who is

STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
Explosion of Ammunitions in the Ammunition Depot, Bharatpur 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES): Sir, 
Ammunition Depot, Bharatpur was established during the period 1957- 65 and 
is located approximately six kms. from Bharatpur town. This Depot holds parts 
of Southern Command Reserve and some portions of Army Headquarters 
Reserve ammunition. The Depot was holding approximately 30,000 tonnes of 
ammunition under both permanent (17,220 metric tonnes) as well as non 
standard storage (12,700 metric tonnes). 
The sequence of events as reported by the Army Headquarters is as 
follows:- 
229 

[ 02 May, 2000 ] RAJYA SABHA 
(a) The fire had started at approximately 1530 hrs. on 28th 
April, 2000, from outside the perimeter wall. 
(b) High temperatures ranging from 45 to 47 degrees Celsius 
and prevailing strong South Westerly winds aided the rapid 
spread of fire to the open plinths. 
(c) The explosion and fire continued unabated throu ghout the 
night of 28/29 April, 2000. The periodicity of explosion 
gradually reduced during the day on 29th April, 2000. 
Finally, the fire was brought under control by the evening of 
29th April, 2000. There has been no explosion since 2200 
hours on 29th April, 2000. 
(d) The Chief of Staff, Headquarters Corps located at Mathura 
was asked to coordinate fire fighting efforts and all available 
resources at Bharatpur, and additional resources from 
Alwar, Agra and Mathura were placed at his disposal. 
While detailed assessment is being made separately, on 29th April, 
2000, the area was reconnoitered. It is confirmed that ammunition stores in 20 
Open Plinths and 9 affected sheds weighing approximately 12111 MT and 
costing about Rs.376 crores was lost. In addition, infrastructure of replacement 
cost of approximately Rs. 13 crores has also been destroyed/damaged. The 
ammunition in the remaining storage sheds is prima facie safe but this would 
need confirmation after detailed inspection. 
Types of Ammunition Stored in this depot are (a) Air Defence 
Missiles (b) Anti Tank Guided Missiles (c) Artillery ammunition of all types (d) 
Tank and BMP ammunition (e) Small Arms ammunition, and (f) Mines and 
explosives. 
As per information available, 2 civilians died and 7 were injured. The 
State Government have been asked by the Ministry for a report on damage to 
life and property. They are in the process of surveying this damage and have 
informed the Ministry on 1.5.2000 that their report will be sent in about a 
week's time. Compensation will be paid for the damages caused, within 7 
days of receipt of proposal from the Government of Rajasthan.  Three Army 
personnel have also been suffered minor injuries. 
230 

RAJYA SABHA [ 02 May, 2000 ] 
The following steps have been taken: - (i) Court of I nquiry under a 
Major General has been constituted; (ii) Adequate qualified personnel to 
inspect remaining ammunition sheds in the depot have been ordered to be 
moved. 
The existing security and safety guidelines are: - (a) A broad policy 
letter regarding pre cautions to be taken to prevent fire accidents with the 
onset of summer was issued on 28th April, 1997, and repromulgated on 17th 
April, 2000. (b) Each ammunition depot has its own security and fire fighting 
instructions which are updated periodically, (c)  Annual inspections are 
undertaken by technical as well as administrative heads, (d) Between 1996-97 
up to 31.3.2000, Rs. 241. 73 crores were allocated for building standard 
storage accommodation. Out of this, Rs. 126.25 crores were sanctioned in 
1999-2000.

very sad development, and our hearts go out to those who have lost their lives 
and to those whose properties hav e been damaged. And I do hope that the 
Government would take speedy action to provide relief to the affected families 
and also to those whose houses have been damaged. I think they need urgent 
attention. 
Sir, this accident or incident also brings out the sad state in which our 
Ammunition/Ordnance Depots are being managed. Scary stories are 
appearing in the newspapers. And I say with great regret that the hon. Minister 
has not clarified many issues which, in the last three or four days, have been 
highlighted in the Press. Therefore, Sr, I will seek specific clarifications on 
specific points. I note that a Court of Inquiry has been ordered, and I do hope 
that this would be a genuine inquiry, that the Government would not try to pre-
judge the whole issue. In this context, Sir, I draw your attention to the fact that 
according to the PTI, the National Security Advisor, Shri Brajesh Mishra, has 
told reporters in Patiala, "As per his information, there was no evidence of 
sabotage." And he is reported to have said, " What we understand is that the 
fire was caused by the negligence of the local labourers." 
I would like to know from the hon. Defence Minister whether he 
shares this view and that if there was negligence, it was only the negligence of 
the labourers. That is  the first point. Sir, the second issue that I do want to 
raise is that, judging from the reports in the Press, a controversy has arisen 
about the methods of storage of explosives. The Army, of course, has denied 
that there was any lapse in storage. But doubts continue to persist. 
Newspapers have reported that more than 60 per cent of the Army's 
ammunition does not have a proper storage facility and lies in the open, in 
more than 15 major ordnance depots spread all over the country. Ammunition 
storage continues to be primitive, under tarpaulin tents. Sir, there have been 
accidents involving fire in the 1980s — I think there was a similar accident at 
Phoolgaon and at Jabalpur -- and the courts of enquiry, at that time, had 
recommended that all ammunition should be stored under covered roof. Sir, 
why has this not been done, despite all the recommendations made by the 
previous courts of enquiry?   This is one 
256 

RAJYA SABHA [ 02 May, 2000 ] 
issue on which I would like to seek a clarification. Sir, 1 understand that the 
court of enquiry for Phoolgaon had stated that elephant grass should not be 
allowed to grow in the vicinity of ordnance depots and ammunition, and 
arrangements be made to instal fire alarm system and automatic water 
sprinkler system.. Apparently,  these recommendations have not been 
implemented. If so, why not? Will the Government assure the House that, 
hereafter, every effort will be made to ensure that ammunition is stored in 
proper ammunition depots? Sir, newspapers have also reported that the 
normal procedure is to cut the grass every year, during the first three months 
of the year, before the onset of summer. Yet it appears that this routine annual 
exercise was not carried out during the last two years. If so, why was grass 
not cut, in accordance with the established procedure in the past two years? 
Reports have appeared that grass inside the depot was as high as seven feet, 
making it impossible for those seeking to control the fire to be successful in 
their efforts. Sir, I understand that elephant grass is excellent for camouflage. 
But 1 also learn from newspaper reports that rules also say that there have to 
be fire lanes 30 feet between stacks and note that no vegetation growth should 
be permitted nearby. This is what the rules per force, say. If not, why not? Sir, 
yet another issue is, the Government's estimate of the toss of ammunition. 
The hon. Minister has mentioned a figure of about Rs. 316 crores. 
Newspapers have mentioned figures ranging between Rs. 2000 and Rs.6000 
crores. I would like the hon. Minister to inform the House as to what is the true 
state of affairs. Newspapers have also reports about the effect of this accident 
on the country's defence preparedness. 1 would like the hon. Minister to 
assure the House that there will be no su ch effect; and if there is any effect, 
how do they propose to remedy the situation? Sir, yet another question is the 
Government's estimate of the loss of human life, cattle and civilian property. It 
has been reported that the Government has not been prompt  enough in 
announcing generous relief to the victims, to the families of the dead and 
wounded and those who have lost their property, crop and cattle. 
What action does the Government propose to take? We would like 
to know this from the hon. Minister. Newspapers have also reported that 
several people have lost their houses in the surrounding villages. What 
measures does the Government contemplate to find solution to the problems 
of finding shelters for those who have been rendered homeless in peak 
summer months in the desert of Rajasthan?   Sir, newspapers have also

reported that unexploded or partially exploded shells are to be found in several 
surrounding areas. The Government, therefore, has to ensure that combing for 
unexploded or partially exploded shells has to be thorough and villagers 
cooperation should be insisted to see to it that these exploded or partially 
exploded shells are retrieved without any further loss of time. This accident 
has caused a good deal of anxiet y in other areas where ammunition depots 
are located. I think this morning the Tribune reported the nervousness that 
prevails in a similar depot in a place near Ludhiana. So. I think safety 
arrangements in and around ammunition depots, therefore, require t he top-
most attention of the Government. I would like the hon. Minister to tell this 
House what measures does he propose to take to give the needed top- priority 
to the questions or issues related to safety around places where ammunition 
depots are located. 
SHRI EDUARDO FALEIRO (Goa): Sir, unfortunately, it has not 
happened for the first time that this type of accident has hit our ammunition 
depot. We had such accidents earlier also. We are an accident -prone society. 
We have accidents in railways; we have ac cidents on roads and everywhere. 
Unfortunately, we are quite notorious in this — we and Pakistan for that 
matter, and Pakistan even more so. Some years ago, there was an accident in 
a Pakistani ammunition dump near Islamabad and more than a thousand 
persons died and many more were injured. So, in these two societies, being 
accident-prone as they are, we are now going in for nuclear weapons as has 
been declared. I would like to know from the hon. Minister as to how we intend 
to cope with safety measures that  are required in a nuclear -weapon situation, 
where it can be a total calamity. This is what I really want to pose here to the 
hon. Minister.

there is an Explosives Act in the country. If there is one. I want to know 
whether these depots are also brought under this Act or not. If they are 
governed by that Act.   there is  a complete prescription given in that as to

how these depots should be maintained. Why the Defence organisations, 
whichever is responsible, have not really looked after this aspect properly, 
under the Act? If not, what action would the Minister take against them? I 
understand, when the storage was done, it was done the way Lord Give had

In his own statement, he said that it is 6 km away from Bharatpur

many more people and property. What our hon. Minister proposes to do? It is 
very risky. He should see to it that such kind of things do not happen, not only

recommendations made by the inquiry committee. What has happened to

the depots? Or are these recommendations kept only in storage?

Sir, their houses have been damaged and even some children are missing. 
The Government has not mentioned about this in the statement. A number of

civilians going to be treated indifferently? How are you going to instil 
confidence in those people so that they can come back to their houses again? 
Do you have any records as to how many houses have been damaged 
because somewhere in the statement the hon. Minister has mentioned that 
after the State Government gives information   as to what

unwanted people such as criminals. What precautions is the Government

pictures where some individuals are taking some kind of artillery or some

Government asked for some compensation? If not, when they ask, within what 
time are they going to be compensated? Some storage sheds are still
